title: B2B relationship management: Customer context for support teams | Pylon
summary: Learn about B2B customer relationship management and how to sync your CRM with your support platform to give teams shared account context.
body_markdown:
For B2B companies, customer relationship management (CRM) is more than just a database of contacts and deals. It’s a tool that helps pre and post-sales teams to give customers a consistent experience.


You can build a stronger shared account context by connecting CRM and customer support systems. That way, support teams can see details about stakeholders and interactions across the account, and customer success can see support activity in the CRM.


In this article, we’ll look at the role of customer relationship management in B2B customer support, then explore how to build a unified account view in practice.


## What’s a B2B CRM and how is it different from B2C?


A B2B CRM is a set of processes, data, and technology that companies use to manage account relationships throughout the customer lifecycle.


Teams from customer success to finance use CRM platforms. While a sales rep might use your CRM system to track leads and log calls, your[customer support team](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-support-strategy) might use it to track service-level agreements (SLAs), spot recurring issues for particular customers, and record issues and resolutions. The system updates in real time, so all these teams have a shared view of account data for each customer.


A B2C CRM focuses on individual relationships with consumers. In B2C, the sales cycle is usually much shorter, and CRM tools often focus on high-volume lead qualification and marketing automation. A B2B CRM needs to track complex relationships involving multiple stakeholders over the long term, so B2B CRM solutions focus on long-term customer retention and relationship building.


## Key features of B2B CRMs


Account notebook editing view from Pylon


These are the core features to look for in B2B CRM platforms:


- **Account hierarchies.** Your team needs to understand how each customer’s company and associated parent/child accounts are structured with a map of different locations and subsidiaries and all the teams within them.
- **Contact roles.** Your team needs to know who the decision-makers are, who the end users are, and how their priorities differ. The CRM should differentiate those roles.
- **Pipeline and deal data.** The CRM should flag the account’s retention status, so support teams can understand the stakes of each support issue and can tailor each conversation to the wider context.
- **Workflow automation.** Modern CRM software should be able to automate routine tasks like scheduling follow-ups and sending[customer feedback surveys](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-feedback-surveys) .
- **Reporting and analytics.** Your CRM stores a mass of valuable customer data, so it should also help you see insights from that data by creating custom dashboards.
- **Integrations.** A CRM isn’t a siloed system; it needs to be connected to your[support platform](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/b2b-customer-service-best-practices-strategies) and other systems so that it can become part of everyday customer conversations.


## Why B2B CRM matters for customer support


Without the right visibility, support teams miss important context. They might have to ask the customer for background information that's already been shared, or give a generic response that may not be appropriate (like sending a technical explanation to a senior executive looking for a high-level overview).


A CRM helps companies avoid these problems by giving everyone access to the same information. Team members can see who they’re talking to and how that person fits into the customer’s[organizational structure](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/business-operations-structure) , as well as a full history of previous interactions and other relevant account context.


With all of this information accessible, support team members can respond more quickly and give more helpful, personalized answers. The CRM supports smoother, context-rich handoffs by giving every team a shared view of the issue when a complex issue needs cross-team coordination. A CRM is important in B2B markets because most customer interactions involve multiple stakeholders across several communication channels.


Just as a CRM benefits the support team, it also benefits other teams when support activity gets recorded. Customer success and sales teams can see open issues and support metrics ahead of an important renewal conversation, helping them to anticipate possible questions and highlight achievements.


## What gets in the way of a unified customer view?


Account custom fields view from Pylon


When support, success, and sales teams don’t store their data in a shared platform like a CRM, visibility fragments quickly. Reporting becomes less reliable, and handoffs leave out important information.


In those situations, team members have to spend their time recreating existing data and searching for context during every interaction. Customers receive inconsistent answers from different teams and may have to repeat themselves for each new point of contact, which builds frustration over time. Some tickets may even fall through the cracks because task ownership isn’t clear.


When a CRM’s data is that fragmented, team members may even go back to relying on individual systems and manual workarounds to find what they need.


## How to build a unified account view


Follow this process to build an effective B2B CRM strategy based on shared account visibility:


- **Define the scope.** List the specific customer information that teams need to share, like conversation details, account hierarchies, and stakeholder roles.
- **Standardize key data.** Create CRM fields that store all of your customer data and specify the format they should be entered in. Consistent formatting makes it much easier for people to find the information they need and for the CRM to integrate with your other programs.
- **Plan integrations.** Choose a platform that provides deep integrations between the CRM, support, success, and other relevant systems, so all customer interactions feed into a[shared account view](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/b2b-customer-service-best-practices-strategies) . These integrations need to sync in both directions; CRM data flows into the support platform, and support conversations are recorded in the CRM.
- **Build shared dashboards.** Decide on the key metrics that should be visible across teams. Build custom dashboards to make metrics like sales pipeline data, account health scores, and[customer satisfaction scores (CSATs)](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-satisfaction-score) instantly available to CRM users.
- **Create accountability.** Establish a clear process for keeping the CRM updated with defined ownership for each step so the information stays accurate and useful.


## Turn customer data into usable account context


Your CRM holds every detail of an account’s story, but building a CRM and populating it with customer data is just the first step. To make a CRM useful, you need to connect it to your support platform so that customer support, success, and sales all have shared access to the account context they need. When the CRM is integrated with other systems, it’s easier to use and easier to maintain.

## FAQ


### What’s B2B customer relationship management?


A B2B customer relationship management (CRM) is a system where companies record interactions and share account data. It gives teams shared visibility into customer context for more personalized, accurate conversations.


### What should companies look for when choosing a B2B CRM?


Prioritize features that are important for sharing information, like customizable fields for account hierarchies and contact roles, and integrations that sync both ways.


### What common mistakes should companies avoid with B2B CRM?


Some common mistakes companies make include rolling out a CRM without input from every team that relies on its data and adding too many custom fields that become difficult to maintain.


### Who should own CRM data in a B2B company?


Overall data ownership should sit with the sales or revenue operations teams, but each team should be responsible for maintaining and updating the data they rely on. For example, the support team should own the process of keeping issue histories and resolution details updated in the CRM.
